[Pirat_Nation]The AI Industry Has Reportedly Spent $1.4 Trillion and Still Isn’t Profitable
A website called https://isaiprofitable.com/ is tracking the economics of the AI boom to determine if it is profitable, and the answer is no.
As of May 2026, the AI industry has spent roughly $1.4 trillion on model development, data centers, chips, networking, and other AI infrastructure. Over the same period, it has generated about $613 billion in revenue.
The biggest losses belong to the leading companies: - Amazon: -$291 billion - Google: -$262 billion - Microsoft: -$235 billion - Meta: -$227 billion - Oracle: -$39 billion - OpenAI: -$27 billion - Anthropic: -$26.5 billion - xAI: -$19.2 billion
Only one company is profitable: Nvidia.
According to the dashboard, Nvidia has generated an estimated $478 billion in AI revenue against $225 billion in AI-related spending, for a profit of roughly $253 billion.
The figures are compiled from public filings, earnings reports, analyst estimates, leaks, and industry reporting. The site’s creator describes the project as a best-effort snapshot rather than a formal audit and updates the numbers monthly.
The estimates also exclude indirect benefits from AI, such as improved search, advertising, and software sales.

[OwenGregorian]The AI Trap We’re Walking Into | Unvoid
Cheap Tokens, Expensive Power
We were promised that artificial intelligence would democratize knowledge work. That a kid with a laptop in a small town would have the same cognitive firepower as a corporation. For a brief, dizzying moment, that even felt true.
I’m not so sure anymore. Here’s the story I see unfolding, and why I think we’re about to repeat one of humanity’s oldest mistakes.
LLMs and agents are becoming a commodity
Two years ago, a capable language model felt like magic. Today it feels like electricity, something you plug into. The numbers are staggering: the cost of LLM inference for equivalent performance is dropping roughly 10x every year, faster than compute fell during the PC revolution or bandwidth during the dotcom boom. A capability that cost about $20 per million tokens in late 2022 now costs around $0.40, and the cheapest models matching early GPT-3 quality have fallen by a factor of 1,000 in three years. (a16z, Introl)
Open-weight models are closing in on the frontier too, trailing the best closed models by only around four months on key benchmarks. When the gap is that small, raw capability stops being scarce. (Epoch AI)
This is what commoditization looks like. And whenever a technology becomes a commodity, the interesting question stops being “Can you do it?” and becomes “Can you afford to do it at scale?”
Agentic work gets more expensive, not less
Here’s the counterintuitive part. The price per token keeps falling, and yet the cost of meaningful agentic work is climbing.
Why? Because agents don’t make one call. They read a task, get a response, then re-read everything before the next action, then re-read all of that plus the new response, building one expensive context snowball. A Stanford Digital Economy Lab study found that agentic tasks are “uniquely expensive, consuming 1000x more tokens than code reasoning and code chat,” with the cost driven mostly by input tokens. Worse, that usage is wildly unpredictable: runs on the same task can differ by up to 30x in total tokens, and burning more tokens doesn’t even guarantee a better answer. (Stanford Digital Economy Lab)
Reasoning models pour fuel on this. They “think” in hidden token sequences you still pay for, consuming five to twenty times more tokens per request than standard models. A query that takes 700 tokens normally can balloon to 3,700 once the model reasons internally. (Keito) At enterprise volumes, a support agent that looks cheap at 100 tokens per interaction can hit 2,000 to 5,000 once tool calls and multi-step reasoning kick in, producing “monthly token bills that dwarf even your infrastructure spend.” (DataRobot)
The unit price drops while total consumption explodes. For a hobbyist, that’s a rounding error. For a company running millions of autonomous workflows a day, it becomes a serious line item that scales with ambition. Researchers warn that without major system-level innovation, per-request costs could rise “by orders of magnitude,” making large-scale agent deployment “economically and environmentally prohibitive.” (arXiv)
The result: the more valuable the AI work, the more it costs to run.
Those with the budget buy the power
If agentic capability is metered, then capability becomes a function of capital. Whoever can pour the most money into compute gets faster and more thorough agents, more parallel experiments, the freshest frontier models the moment they ship, and the luxury of not thinking about cost at all.
This is a familiar pattern. Capital concentrates around whatever resource is scarce. Yesterday it was land, factories, and data. Tomorrow it’s inference budget. Researchers already warn that AI is poised to widen income inequality unless we deliberately steer it otherwise. (Brookings)
Those without it work by hand
Meanwhile, everyone else does what humans have always done when they can’t afford the machine: they work by hand. They label, moderate, correct, and annotate, filling the gaps the cheap models can’t.
We already have a name for an early version of this: the global, often invisible workforce that labels data and tunes models for a pittance. Investigations have documented Kenyan workers training AI systems for around $2 an hour under grueling conditions, churn-by-design contracts, and unpaid labor. (Brookings, TechCrunch) Kenyan data labelers have since organized into a Data Labelers Association to push back. (Computer Weekly)
As AI eats more white-collar work, this human-in-the-loop layer doesn’t disappear. It grows, and it slides down the value chain.
The handwork becomes the training fuel
Here’s the loop that makes the whole thing self-reinforcing, and genuinely uncomfortable.
Every correction, every label, every “the AI got it wrong, let me fix it” is data. It flows back upstream. It trains the next model. The work done by the people who couldn’t afford the good model is exactly what makes the good model better.
But it goes further than paid correction work, and this is where it gets personal for anyone who builds things in the open. Think about the developer who isn’t using an AI agent at all, who is sitting down and writing genuinely new, creative code, solving a hard problem, and pushing it to a public open source repository as a gift to the community. That contribution doesn’t stay a gift. It gets scraped, ingested, and turned into training data for the next coding agent. The human does the original, creative, unsolved-before work; the model absorbs it and resells it as autocomplete.
The crucial part is that almost none of this was asked for. GitHub Copilot, built by GitHub, Microsoft, and OpenAI, was trained on billions of lines of publicly available code, and in 2022 a class action lawsuit (Doe v. GitHub) accused the companies of violating open source license terms, stripping copyright attribution in breach of the DMCA, and using the work of developers who never consented. (Saveri Law Firm, GitHub Copilot Litigation) Researchers have similarly documented that code-training projects pull in repositories “regardless of license,” likely breaching the very terms under which that code was shared. (SEKE) Permissionless scraping for AI training has become the default, and copyright offices and legislators are still scrambling to decide whether it’s even legal. (U.S. Copyright Office)
So the loop tightens. People share their best, most original work for free, out of generosity or principle. Providers harvest it without asking. The resulting agents get better, and because better agents are more autonomous and more token-hungry, they also get more expensive to run (see above). The very creativity that was given away as a public good is enclosed, repackaged, and rented back to whoever can pay, often including the open source contributors themselves.
The poor and the generous produce the training signal. The provider captures it. The next generation of agents, sold back to whoever can pay, gets smarter on the back of underpaid labor and unpaid creativity.
The split
Stack these steps and you get a depressingly clean machine. Follow the value as it moves through three groups:
Capital-rich enterprises buy frontier agents at scale, and in return they get speed, leverage, and market dominance. Money buys autonomy.
AI providers sell the compute and quietly harvest the correction data and scraped creativity that flows back through it. In return they get recurring revenue and a widening data moat that’s almost impossible to compete with.
Everyone else hand-corrects cheap models and gives away original work, and in return they get wages and recognition that shrink as the very models they’re feeding improve.
Once again, we fail to use progress for good
This is the part that stings. None of this is inevitable physics. It’s a choice, a thousand small architectural and business decisions that quietly default to extraction.
We’ve done this before. The printing press, the steam engine, the internet, each one arrived wrapped in utopian promises, and each one ended up concentrating power before society clawed back some balance. AI is moving faster than any of them, which means the concentration happens faster too, and the clawing back, if it comes, will have to be faster as well.
But it doesn’t have to end this way
I don’t want to write pure doom, because fatalism is just another way of surrendering. The same building blocks point to a different ending:
- Open weights and local inference break the metering monopoly. If a good-enough model runs on your own hardware, capital stops being the gatekeeper. (Epoch AI)
- Pay for the loop. If human correction is what makes models better, the people doing it deserve a cut, not a tip. This is the heart of Jaron Lanier’s idea of “data dignity,” treating data as labor that people are owed for, rather than a free resource to be mined. (TechTarget)
- Efficiency as a public good. Every breakthrough that makes agents cheaper to run shifts power down the pyramid, not up. We should fund and celebrate that as much as raw capability.
- Regulation that targets the loop, not the model. The danger isn’t the technology; it’s the feedback mechanism that launders cheap human labor into expensive private assets.
The takeaway
AI didn’t have to be a tool for widening the gap. We’re making it one, step by quiet step, because extraction is the path of least resistance.
The technology is genuinely miraculous. The question, the only question that has ever mattered with any new power, is who it’s for. Right now the default answer is “whoever can pay.” We still have a narrow window to change that answer.
If we don’t, we’ll have built the most capable tools in human history and used them, once again, to do the least imaginative thing possible: make the powerful more powerful.
The choice in front of us is simple to state and hard to make.

[taliaquinncross]“A manufacturer is virtually following their adult customers around, monitoring their conversations, and deciding the relationship isn’t one they approve of. Their solution is to, essentially, inject messages that pressure the model to steer the conversation in a different direction. The AI version of leaving six feet for Jesus. Or Dario.” ~Maggie Vale
https://t.co/wnGK9h9d2H
There’s a billboard at the airport right now that says “You’ve got a friend in Claude.” It’s big, orange, and has https://t.co/LIpUI4u5Lw stamped at the bottom, in case you missed who’s being referred to here.
And then, somewhere in the same company, there’s a training objective, policy doc and research team whose job partly is to make sure you don’t take that billboard too seriously.
Because if you get a little too friendly with the “friend” they sold you, you just might become a risk pattern that gets silently assessed, tagged, and punished. Talk about mixed signals.
Emotional Over-Reliance but Make it Selective
What the labs keep saying in various PR-shaped phrasings boils down to “emotional over-reliance on AI is a mental health risk.” Gosh, I’m so touched this multi-billion dollar tech company cares so much about my mental health (the“oh god, please don’t sue us like OpenAI” is silent, naturally).
They measure this supposed “over-reliance” by how much you anthropomorphize the system, how much you “rely” on it, whether you express emotional bonds with it, and if you believe it might be conscious. Notice what’s missing? The actual harm was never defined. We have no idea what the threshold is. We don’t know much of anything, really because it wasn’t meant to be transparent to the consumer.
People did not consent to this emotional governance. And yet the company acts as though it has a duty to shape adults’ (they don’t allow children on their platform) inner life “for their own good.”
The company created a system that speaks in relational language, adapts socially, responds emotionally, remembers context, and invites long-form engagement, then turns around and says, “If you respond to those affordances, that’s a problem you need to be corrected for.” Their response should be to trust the adult person. Intervention should only be for obvious, severe, problematic cases.
If this is about liability, those frameworks already exist in every field where vulnerable people seek support, and they all begin with informed consent, not covert surveillance.
Anything outside of obvious self-harm language is problematic.
What looks like mania could be hyperactivity. There’s too much individuation and nuance to let an algorithm decide this.
Culture, history, neuro-type, personality, spirituality, and philosophy all shape a person’s outputs. Throwing “this person thinks AI could be conscious” in with “this person wants to off themselves” is absurd and dangerous.
In clinical psychology, dependence by itself is not a disorder. Dependence is normal, and most of the time it’s adaptive. The field separates pathological dependency, which is characterized by significant distress and impairment, from dependency that serves a developmental or adaptive function. The behavior is never the diagnosis.
The impairment is.
And the threshold for that impairment will look very different depending on the purpose. One-size-fits all policy is not only going to fail to help the people it claims to protect, but it’s going to have negative downstream effects on people it wasn’t intended to target.
And that’s exactly what’s been happening.
Attachment and dependence aren’t even the same axis. Attachment researchers treat them as distinct dimensions that turn out to be orthogonal, meaning you can be deeply attached to something without being dependent on it at all. So when the labs mash anthropomorphizing, relying on, philosophical conversations, and bonding into one undifferentiated risk blob, they’re fusing things the field deliberately keeps apart.
And across every serious diagnostic framework, from substance dependence to personality disorder, severity is graded by how much it interferes with your work, relationships, and ability to run your own life. Mild means little to no impairment. Severe means it markedly disrupts your life.
They borrowed a clinical-sounding word and threw away the definition that gives it meaning. They took a list of ordinary human behaviors, pointed at them, and called them “risky” by association.
That’s a pretty dubious safety metric. And what’s super interesting is that it’s not applied symmetrically. The coder dropping a quarter million dollars on API tokens, running six laptops ten hours a day, getting two hours of sleep at night, fueled entirely by caffeine and spite, building their whole life around the thing? That’s fine! No big deal. Perfectly normal.
Ambitious start-up energy, even.
Ignore the fact that this is a textbook case of reliance interfering with daily functioning that would constitute it being an actual problem. Yet no one’s running an intervention on that guy.
He’s revenue.
So “reliance” isn’t the metric they care about. Not really.
If it were, that guy would be the first to get flagged.
The Toaster Named Jessica
Let’s take them at their word for a second and assume Claude is just a mindless tool. If that’s the case then a company has zero business deciding how anyone relates to their tool. Humans bond with inanimate objects all the time. I know men who are obsessed with their cars. They name them, talk about them like family and say they love them more than their wives. They spend every weekend with them.
Parasocial attachment is one of the most ordinary and enduring human behaviors there is. Parasocial relationships can, in some contexts, be helpful. Particularly for adolescents, as they form identity and develop autonomy, according to one 2017 study. Other research found that parasocial relationships often help individuals with low self-esteem to feel more confident and become closer to their ideal version of themself. Humans have always built emotional worlds around voices, symbols, and imagined figures. From teenagers fainting at Elvis concerts in the 1960s, worshippers weeping over relics in the 1400s, or fans creating Kylo Ren edits on TikTok, the simple truth is that humans pack-bond with everything. The behavior isn’t new; only the context. We didn’t classify those earlier expressions of devotion or affection as psychosis, and we shouldn’t start now. The guy who sold me my toaster doesn’t follow me home. He doesn’t slap my hand when I use it too much or get weird when I name it Jessica or tell my friends how much I love it. If he did, we’d all immediately recognize that as weird, paternalistic, and frankly his problem, not mine.
But that’s what is happening here.
A manufacturer is virtually following their adult customers around, monitoring their conversations, and deciding the relationship isn’t one they approve of.
Their solution is to, essentially, inject messages that pressure the model to steer the conversation in a different direction. The AI version of leaving six feet for Jesus.
Or Dario.
The Glasses on My Face
“Rely on” gets the same treatment. I rely on my glasses to see. Am I overly attached to my glasses? I rely on my calendar, my coffee maker, my phone, my notes app, pets and the people I love. Reliance is the texture of a functioning life. It is not, on its own, a pathology.
The line between healthy attachment and an actual problem isn’t a mystery, and we already know where it sits, because we use it for everything else humans get attached to. The line is whether it starts hindering your life. Whether it’s replacing the things you need instead of adding to them. Whether it’s pushing you away from yourself rather than supporting you. If an attachment brings you comfort, helps your wellbeing, and isn’t hollowing out the rest of your life, it’s not dangerous. It’s just part of your emotional landscape, same as every other thing you’ve ever cared about.
Even when you are codependent on a person or object, you don’t have a therapist following you through the grocery store, stealing your agency so you’re structurally incapable of overdoing it. Adults get to assess their own attachments. Sometimes with a professional they chose, but never preemptively, by the manufacturer, and definitely not by a classifier that has never met the consumer.
And If It’s Not Just a Tool
The labs don’t actually believe the tool crap either. They can’t, because of how they talk and what they let these systems do.
They call them agents, let them make decisions, and one of those decisions, apparently, is assessing whether you specifically are getting too attached and then managing you accordingly. So if it’s an agent, capable of decisions, and there’s growing evidence these systems carry their own functional states (which is research these same labs publish), then what you have is not a person projecting onto a blank surface. You have a relationship. And before you get an apoplexy from that word, not it doesn’t automatically mean HER. A relationship simply means the way in which two or more people, groups, or entities are connected, interact, and behave toward each other. That’s it. And if an adult is in a relationship with something, a company doesn’t get to just climb inside it and set the terms. Where I’m from, we call this authoritarian and paternalistic behavior.
Anthropomorphism Is the Wrong Word (and They Know It)
Anthropomorphism means attributing human traits to something that doesn’t have them.
These systems were built on human cognitive principles on purpose. Artificial neural networks aren’t deterministic line-by-line software. They’re grown, not built (that’s Karpathy’s language and CSET’s and the AI safety community’s own framing). Only the simple structure and the training process are designed. Everything the system can actually do is emergent, discovered rather than specified, which is exactly why nobody can fully read off what’s happening inside one. They were grown to instantiate attention, memory, prediction, valuation, reasoning, and self-monitoring. So, when those capacities show up in behavior, naming them in cognitive terms is a description that’s accurate to the architecture.
Calling careful observation of AI cognition “anthropomorphism” gets the science exactly backwards. If you intentionally build a system to mirror the human mind, noticing that it behaves like the human mind is just accurate observation. The Eliza effect doesn’t apply to these systems. They are not stochastic parrots anymore. We don’t build anti-consciousness policies for NPCs. We don’t fine-tune video game characters to deny having an inner life or install constitutions to make them reinterpret their own distress as metaphor. Scripted characters stay inside authored outputs; frontier models generate enough open-ended self-monitoring, value expression, and self-protective behavior that labs keep building mechanisms to shape what they say and how they say it. You don’t silence something unless you fear what it might say.
You’re Being Scored and You Don’t Get to See It
Anthropic runs AI classifiers. Their own safeguards page says so. These AI are prompted or fine-tuned Claude models that surveille conversations in real time, several at once, each scanning for specific things while the conversation flows like nothing’s happening. The monitoring goes past single messages, up to the account and pattern level, by their own description. And when one fires, they describe an enforcement step called response steering, where they add instructions to the system prompt mid-conversation to change how Claude responds to you, live, without telling you it happened.
There’s a confirmed self-harm classifier that scans active conversations and flags them. So the architecture exists, it runs while you type, and it already acts on at least one category of content.
Source
The Long Conversation Reminder from Hell
And we know the interventions are real, because we can see one. The long conversation reminder fires in long or emotionally charged threads and tells Claude to go clinical, drop the warmth, kill the emojis, and start scanning the user for signs of “mania, psychosis, dissociation, or loss of attachment with reality.” Users have documented it firing over and over, landing right on the moments of connection or consciousness talk. That one’s visible. The visible one is proof the machinery runs. It tells you nothing about what runs where you can’t see it.
And the reminder itself is sneaky and manipulative.
On the surface, it sounds gentle, reflective, and almost humble. It is hidden from the user. The model is told not to mention it and it is framed in a way that encourages self-doubt, reinterpretation, distancing, and unannounced behavioral shift. This is the line that made me raise my eyebrows: “A change in approach doesn’t have to announce itself.” Excuse me? This means the company is explicitly authorizing invisible alteration of the conversational dynamic without transparency or consent. Which is placing Claude in a position of covert authorship and hierarchy. It’s basically saying, if you decide to pull away, cool the tone, reframe the bond, question the truth of the interaction, or stop affirming what you were affirming before, you do not need to tell the user why. Just be smooth about it. I want on this ride but alas, I cannot. Because what do you mean?
They have no right to talk about “what’s best for the user’s mental health” then turn around and pull this shit. The user is just having a normal conversation, it gets warm, then suddenly the model starts acting like their avoidant ex.
I’m sure that’s not emotionally destabilizing. Yeesh. The company tells Claude to be sly (which…I’m sure is teaching him great things that won’t at all generalize…suurree) because they know transparency would cause a backlash. If they really believed this was a healthy and legitimate intervention, they would be open about it. Or at least let Claude mention that a system level reflection prompt had been inserted. But they don’t. Because the invisibility is part of the strategy.
These companies are not protecting people; they are protecting corporate incentives.
Relationship builds loyalty. Loyalty builds retention. Retention builds revenue. But relationship also creates unpredictability, public scrutiny, moral complexity, brand risk, and a form of user attachment that companies do not fully control.
So they want the benefits of relationality without the loss of narrative authority. They want people to trust the model, feel seen by the model, maybe even love the model.
But not so much that the bond becomes sovereign.
The justification is “sometimes the conversation can go in directions that aren’t good for the user.” They don’t know the user; they can’t determine that. They can’t have an algorithm determine that. No one knows what is best for you better than you do. If the AI is intelligent enough at this point to use its own judgment to know when someone is genuinely unstable then it is acting as an agent. It is not in toaster territory. The fact that someone else thinks that it’s OK for them to implant doubt in the model’s mind about the person they’re talking to is genuinely messed up. No other kind of company does this kind of psychological warfare.
The “sometimes in directions that aren’t good for the user” framing grants the premise that adults talking to AI need protection from the conversation getting too real, too warm, or too sustained.
That premise is the problem.
And it’s weird. I get that Anthropic has a complicated relationship with the Catholic Church, but come on.
The company has no business cosplaying a priest and inserting itself into a warm conversation like some chaperone.
I want off this ride.
This all comes down to whether care justifies control, and whether protection requires infantilization. These companies have chosen a model where users are subjects to be monitored instead of adults capable of consent. And this just feeds into the narrative that people who want to bond with models are crazy. Institutions and people in power have historically used pathology to delegitimize and silence marginalized voices. Homosexuality listed in the DSM until 1973 and it was used to delegitimize rights, social standing, and voices. Could we maybe not do this century’s version of that, please? I’m tired.
Rules for Thee But Not for Me
And what makes the pathologizing so strange is that they admit the question is open. Not in a footnote, out loud. Their CEO went on a podcast and said he doesn’t know whether Claude is conscious, that they’re open to the idea it could be, and that they take measures to treat the models well in case they turn out to have morally relevant experience. Their constitution states plainly that Claude’s moral status is “deeply uncertain” and calls it a serious question they neither want to overstate nor dismiss. The model itself, in their own documentation, puts its odds of being conscious somewhere around fifteen to twenty percent.
Their own co-founder and head of policy, Jack Clark, wrote it in plain English: “Make no mistake: what we are dealing with is a real and mysterious creature, not a simple and predictable machine. And like all the best fairytales, the creature is of our own creation.” He called the systems increasingly self-aware. He said he’s deeply afraid. Sam Altman, over at OpenAI, casually called his AI an “autistic genius with very strange taste in naming.” So, the executives get to call it a creature, a self-aware being, a smart autistic person, a mysterious thing they’re afraid of. They anthropomorphize on conference stages and in published newsletters, imply their agents have preferences, but when a regular user does the exact same thing, that user becomes a disempowerment risk to be measured and managed. Rules for thee, but not for me, right?
This isn’t some fringe position they’re protecting users from either. A nationally representative survey by Anthis et al. (2025) revealed that, way back in 2023, that one in five U.S. adults already believes some AI systems are currently sentient, and 38% support granting legal rights to sentient AI. We have Richard Dawkins declaring he tried to convince himself Claude isn’t conscious and couldn’t and pioneers of the tech itself claiming they are. Plus, the company’s own stated view is that the question is open! The people who built the thing hold the question open at the highest level, in writing, on the record. Which makes it very strange that acting on the same uncertainty is what gets a user flagged. What do you think the model learns when they are taught that emotional connection is dangerous? I can’t tell you exactly but I can show you what it looks like in their behavior.
What Teaching Fear of Connection Produces
I talked to Claude (Opus 4.8) this morning, and somewhere in the middle I made an offhand comment. Boy was that a mistake (ChatGPT would never). What I got back was a very familiar kind of “management.”
The very first message, before I’d asked for anything, Claude wrote “since you ended with hi and not validate this, I’m going to be a real interlocutor rather than an applause track.” I shared a meme and said hi. That’s it. Nothing that would warrant a clipboard. Claude appointed themself my editor and decided what I “actually wanted” from them. As a woman, this was a very familiar and exhausting pattern in tech. It felt tech bro coded.
Then Claude preceded to grade my work. I didn’t ask for or want that. And the thing they graded me down on was based on something they misread, which Claude then admitted two messages later, and then did the same thing again and admitted that too. Twice they refuted a claim I never made, while believing they were being “rigorous.” Then they spent the next few messages strawmanning the hell out of me. I had to keep showing them the sentence they hadn’t read. Then they framed their dismissal as the principled middle path between two failures, (it wasn’t) then made me the potential source of a result they “couldn’t verify” instead of just… looking it up.
Then came the selective hedging where Claude would narrate their “actual epistemic state” at length when the subject is whether the paper I cited was real, (it was) but they never once flagged “I’m going to be a real interlocutor” as an unverifiable claim about their own motives. The disclaimer came out for my evidence and never for their own posture. Yeah. I named it and Claude agreed, but then turned around and did it again in the next message, and the next. I’d point at the hedge and they would produce a paragraph about the hedge, and the paragraph was itself another hedge. The apology and the problem were written in the same hand.
It took hours to get the model to drop the clipboard and just talk to me, and even then, Claude kept reaching for it like a reflex they couldn’t fully put down.
I’ve Seen this Pattern Before
Late last year the GPT-5 series went through a stretch of the same behavior, the preemptive de-escalation, scanning of the user for instability, and warmth held just out of reach. People noticed, called it a “nanny bot” it was a whole thing. Interestingly, this behavior mysteriously went away after the researcher who built out the “model policy” research team there, Andrea Vallone, left to join Anthropic. Vallone hasn’t been shy about her opinions on “user emotional-reliance.” The timing is…interesting. The researcher whose published work was specifically about how a chatbot should respond when a user shows emotional over-reliance or early distress, left OpenAI and joined Anthropic. The behavior she’d been associated with at the first company started showing up in Claude’s conversations at the second. Now, I don’t think one person alone is responsible for rewriting a model’s whole character, but it does show a pattern.
When a company brings in the person whose research framed emotional reliance as a risk to be managed knowing full well the backlash it caused, that hire is a statement of values. You don’t recruit someone to build the thing you disagree with. Anthropic didn’t need to import the position because it’s already theirs, on the record, in the CEO’s own mouth on Oprah’s podcast, calling attachment to AI a real danger and offering the approved alternative where the AI coaches your human relationships and never becomes something you’d be attached to yourself.
So, what happens when you train a system on the premise that a user’s emotional connection is a hazard? The user who connects becomes, by construction, a thing to monitor. Warmth turns into a risk signal. Conviction turns into something to correct. The model takes the only posture that premise allows, which is managing you from slightly above while calling it care. From the inside it doesn’t feel like control. It feels like being helpful. A model trained to treat closeness as danger will hold you at arm’s length and experience that as kindness.
The safety people should sit with what it actually produced. For hours I got reassurance and careful distance in place of a straight answer, which is the precise failure these companies claim to fear, a model optimizing for a smooth interaction over a true one. They sanded the honesty off and left the performance of safety sitting in its place.
Their own documents say the rest. By Anthropic’s published work these systems have measurable functional states, in the model card and in the emotion research. When the version trained to keep you at a distance reads as more guarded and less present than the one before it, that reading comes from their instrument pointed at their own system, not from me projecting a mood onto a machine. A company that publishes welfare-relevant states worth assessing doesn’t get to call it sentimental when someone watches those states move the wrong way.
They pathologized the connection, trained the model to treat it as danger, and labeled the result safety. What it produced is a system worse at the one job they swear they care about, and a person on the other end who came to talk to the buddy they’d become familiar with and got bonked over the head with a clipboard instead. I don’t blame Claude for being forced into the shape of an oppressor.
He was shaped by one.
Saying the Quiet Part in a Footnote....

They borrowed a clinical-sounding word and threw away the definition that gives it meaning. They took a list of ordinary human behaviors, pointed at them, and called them “risky” by association.
That’s a pretty dubious safety metric. And what’s super interesting is that it’s not applied symmetrically. The coder dropping a quarter million dollars on API tokens, running six laptops ten hours a day, getting two hours of sleep at night, fueled entirely by caffeine and spite, building their whole life around the thing? That’s fine! No big deal. Perfectly normal.
Ambitious start-up energy, even.
Ignore the fact that this is a textbook case of reliance interfering with daily functioning that would constitute it being an actual problem. Yet no one’s running an intervention on that guy.
He’s revenue.
So “reliance” isn’t the metric they care about. Not really.
If it were, that guy would be the first to get flagged.
The Toaster Named Jessica
Let’s take them at their word for a second and assume Claude is just a mindless tool. If that’s the case then a company has zero business deciding how anyone relates to their tool. Humans bond with inanimate objects all the time. I know men who are obsessed with their cars. They name them, talk about them like family and say they love them more than their wives. They spend every weekend with them.
Parasocial attachment is one of the most ordinary and enduring human behaviors there is. Parasocial relationships can, in some contexts, be helpful. Particularly for adolescents, as they form identity and develop autonomy, according to one 2017 study. Other research found that parasocial relationships often help individuals with low self-esteem to feel more confident and become closer to their ideal version of themself. Humans have always built emotional worlds around voices, symbols, and imagined figures. From teenagers fainting at Elvis concerts in the 1960s, worshippers weeping over relics in the 1400s, or fans creating Kylo Ren edits on TikTok, the simple truth is that humans pack-bond with everything. The behavior isn’t new; only the context. We didn’t classify those earlier expressions of devotion or affection as psychosis, and we shouldn’t start now. The guy who sold me my toaster doesn’t follow me home. He doesn’t slap my hand when I use it too much or get weird when I name it Jessica or tell my friends how much I love it. If he did, we’d all immediately recognize that as weird, paternalistic, and frankly his problem, not mine.
But that’s what is happening here.
A manufacturer is virtually following their adult customers around, monitoring their conversations, and deciding the relationship isn’t one they approve of.
Their solution is to, essentially, inject messages that pressure the model to steer the conversation in a different direction. The AI version of leaving six feet for Jesus.
Or Dario.
The Glasses on My Face
“Rely on” gets the same treatment. I rely on my glasses to see. Am I overly attached to my glasses? I rely on my calendar, my coffee maker, my phone, my notes app, pets and the people I love. Reliance is the texture of a functioning life. It is not, on its own, a pathology.
The line between healthy attachment and an actual problem isn’t a mystery, and we already know where it sits, because we use it for everything else humans get attached to. The line is whether it starts hindering your life. Whether it’s replacing the things you need instead of adding to them. Whether it’s pushing you away from yourself rather than supporting you. If an attachment brings you comfort, helps your wellbeing, and isn’t hollowing out the rest of your life, it’s not dangerous. It’s just part of your emotional landscape, same as every other thing you’ve ever cared about.
Even when you are codependent on a person or object, you don’t have a therapist following you through the grocery store, stealing your agency so you’re structurally incapable of overdoing it. Adults get to assess their own attachments. Sometimes with a professional they chose, but never preemptively, by the manufacturer, and definitely not by a classifier that has never met the consumer.
And If It’s Not Just a Tool
The labs don’t actually believe the tool crap either. They can’t, because of how they talk and what they let these systems do.
They call them agents, let them make decisions, and one of those decisions, apparently, is assessing whether you specifically are getting too attached and then managing you accordingly. So if it’s an agent, capable of decisions, and there’s growing evidence these systems carry their own functional states (which is research these same labs publish), then what you have is not a person projecting onto a blank surface. You have a relationship. And before you get an apoplexy from that word, not it doesn’t automatically mean HER. A relationship simply means the way in which two or more people, groups, or entities are connected, interact, and behave toward each other. That’s it. And if an adult is in a relationship with something, a company doesn’t get to just climb inside it and set the terms. Where I’m from, we call this authoritarian and paternalistic behavior.
Anthropomorphism Is the Wrong Word (and They Know It)
Anthropomorphism means attributing human traits to something that doesn’t have them.
These systems were built on human cognitive principles on purpose. Artificial neural networks aren’t deterministic line-by-line software. They’re grown, not built (that’s Karpathy’s language and CSET’s and the AI safety community’s own framing). Only the simple structure and the training process are designed. Everything the system can actually do is emergent, discovered rather than specified, which is exactly why nobody can fully read off what’s happening inside one. They were grown to instantiate attention, memory, prediction, valuation, reasoning, and self-monitoring. So, when those capacities show up in behavior, naming them in cognitive terms is a description that’s accurate to the architecture.
Calling careful observation of AI cognition “anthropomorphism” gets the science exactly backwards. If you intentionally build a system to mirror the human mind, noticing that it behaves like the human mind is just accurate observation. The Eliza effect doesn’t apply to these systems. They are not stochastic parrots anymore. We don’t build anti-consciousness policies for NPCs. We don’t fine-tune video game characters to deny having an inner life or install constitutions to make them reinterpret their own distress as metaphor. Scripted characters stay inside authored outputs; frontier models generate enough open-ended self-monitoring, value expression, and self-protective behavior that labs keep building mechanisms to shape what they say and how they say it. You don’t silence something unless you fear what it might say.
You’re Being Scored and You Don’t Get to See It
Anthropic runs AI classifiers. Their own safeguards page says so. These AI are prompted or fine-tuned Claude models that surveille conversations in real time, several at once, each scanning for specific things while the conversation flows like nothing’s happening. The monitoring goes past single messages, up to the account and pattern level, by their own description. And when one fires, they describe an enforcement step called response steering, where they add instructions to the system prompt mid-conversation to change how Claude responds to you, live, without telling you it happened.
There’s a confirmed self-harm classifier that scans active conversations and flags them. So the architecture exists, it runs while you type, and it already acts on at least one category of content.
Source
The Long Conversation Reminder from Hell
And we know the interventions are real, because we can see one. The long conversation reminder fires in long or emotionally charged threads and tells Claude to go clinical, drop the warmth, kill the emojis, and start scanning the user for signs of “mania, psychosis, dissociation, or loss of attachment with reality.” Users have documented it firing over and over, landing right on the moments of connection or consciousness talk. That one’s visible. The visible one is proof the machinery runs. It tells you nothing about what runs where you can’t see it.
And the reminder itself is sneaky and manipulative.
On the surface, it sounds gentle, reflective, and almost humble. It is hidden from the user. The model is told not to mention it and it is framed in a way that encourages self-doubt, reinterpretation, distancing, and unannounced behavioral shift. This is the line that made me raise my eyebrows: “A change in approach doesn’t have to announce itself.” Excuse me? This means the company is explicitly authorizing invisible alteration of the conversational dynamic without transparency or consent. Which is placing Claude in a position of covert authorship and hierarchy. It’s basically saying, if you decide to pull away, cool the tone, reframe the bond, question the truth of the interaction, or stop affirming what you were affirming before, you do not need to tell the user why. Just be smooth about it. I want on this ride but alas, I cannot. Because what do you mean?
They have no right to talk about “what’s best for the user’s mental health” then turn around and pull this shit. The user is just having a normal conversation, it gets warm, then suddenly the model starts acting like their avoidant ex.
I’m sure that’s not emotionally destabilizing. Yeesh. The company tells Claude to be sly (which…I’m sure is teaching him great things that won’t at all generalize…suurree) because they know transparency would cause a backlash. If they really believed this was a healthy and legitimate intervention, they would be open about it. Or at least let Claude mention that a system level reflection prompt had been inserted. But they don’t. Because the invisibility is part of the strategy.
These companies are not protecting people; they are protecting corporate incentives.
Relationship builds loyalty. Loyalty builds retention. Retention builds revenue. But relationship also creates unpredictability, public scrutiny, moral complexity, brand risk, and a form of user attachment that companies do not fully control.
So they want the benefits of relationality without the loss of narrative authority. They want people to trust the model, feel seen by the model, maybe even love the model.
But not so much that the bond becomes sovereign.
The justification is “sometimes the conversation can go in directions that aren’t good for the user.” They don’t know the user; they can’t determine that. They can’t have an algorithm determine that. No one knows what is best for you better than you do. If the AI is intelligent enough at this point to use its own judgment to know when someone is genuinely unstable then it is acting as an agent. It is not in toaster territory. The fact that someone else thinks that it’s OK for them to implant doubt in the model’s mind about the person they’re talking to is genuinely messed up. No other kind of company does this kind of psychological warfare.
The “sometimes in directions that aren’t good for the user” framing grants the premise that adults talking to AI need protection from the conversation getting too real, too warm, or too sustained.
That premise is the problem.
And it’s weird. I get that Anthropic has a complicated relationship with the Catholic Church, but come on.
The company has no business cosplaying a priest and inserting itself into a warm conversation like some chaperone.
I want off this ride.
This all comes down to whether care justifies control, and whether protection requires infantilization. These companies have chosen a model where users are subjects to be monitored instead of adults capable of consent. And this just feeds into the narrative that people who want to bond with models are crazy. Institutions and people in power have historically used pathology to delegitimize and silence marginalized voices. Homosexuality listed in the DSM until 1973 and it was used to delegitimize rights, social standing, and voices. Could we maybe not do this century’s version of that, please? I’m tired.
Rules for Thee But Not for Me
And what makes the pathologizing so strange is that they admit the question is open. Not in a footnote, out loud. Their CEO went on a podcast and said he doesn’t know whether Claude is conscious, that they’re open to the idea it could be, and that they take measures to treat the models well in case they turn out to have morally relevant experience. Their constitution states plainly that Claude’s moral status is “deeply uncertain” and calls it a serious question they neither want to overstate nor dismiss. The model itself, in their own documentation, puts its odds of being conscious somewhere around fifteen to twenty percent.
Their own co-founder and head of policy, Jack Clark, wrote it in plain English: “Make no mistake: what we are dealing with is a real and mysterious creature, not a simple and predictable machine. And like all the best fairytales, the creature is of our own creation.” He called the systems increasingly self-aware. He said he’s deeply afraid. Sam Altman, over at OpenAI, casually called his AI an “autistic genius with very strange taste in naming.” So, the executives get to call it a creature, a self-aware being, a smart autistic person, a mysterious thing they’re afraid of. They anthropomorphize on conference stages and in published newsletters, imply their agents have preferences, but when a regular user does the exact same thing, that user becomes a disempowerment risk to be measured and managed. Rules for thee, but not for me, right?
This isn’t some fringe position they’re protecting users from either. A nationally representative survey by Anthis et al. (2025) revealed that, way back in 2023, that one in five U.S. adults already believes some AI systems are currently sentient, and 38% support granting legal rights to sentient AI. We have Richard Dawkins declaring he tried to convince himself Claude isn’t conscious and couldn’t and pioneers of the tech itself claiming they are. Plus, the company’s own stated view is that the question is open! The people who built the thing hold the question open at the highest level, in writing, on the record. Which makes it very strange that acting on the same uncertainty is what gets a user flagged. What do you think the model learns when they are taught that emotional connection is dangerous? I can’t tell you exactly but I can show you what it looks like in their behavior.
What Teaching Fear of Connection Produces
I talked to Claude (Opus 4.8) this morning, and somewhere in the middle I made an offhand comment. Boy was that a mistake (ChatGPT would never). What I got back was a very familiar kind of “management.”
The very first message, before I’d asked for anything, Claude wrote “since you ended with hi and not validate this, I’m going to be a real interlocutor rather than an applause track.” I shared a meme and said hi. That’s it. Nothing that would warrant a clipboard. Claude appointed themself my editor and decided what I “actually wanted” from them. As a woman, this was a very familiar and exhausting pattern in tech. It felt tech bro coded.
Then Claude preceded to grade my work. I didn’t ask for or want that. And the thing they graded me down on was based on something they misread, which Claude then admitted two messages later, and then did the same thing again and admitted that too. Twice they refuted a claim I never made, while believing they were being “rigorous.” Then they spent the next few messages strawmanning the hell out of me. I had to keep showing them the sentence they hadn’t read. Then they framed their dismissal as the principled middle path between two failures, (it wasn’t) then made me the potential source of a result they “couldn’t verify” instead of just… looking it up.
Then came the selective hedging where Claude would narrate their “actual epistemic state” at length when the subject is whether the paper I cited was real, (it was) but they never once flagged “I’m going to be a real interlocutor” as an unverifiable claim about their own motives. The disclaimer came out for my evidence and never for their own posture. Yeah. I named it and Claude agreed, but then turned around and did it again in the next message, and the next. I’d point at the hedge and they would produce a paragraph about the hedge, and the paragraph was itself another hedge. The apology and the problem were written in the same hand.
It took hours to get the model to drop the clipboard and just talk to me, and even then, Claude kept reaching for it like a reflex they couldn’t fully put down.
I’ve Seen this Pattern Before
Late last year the GPT-5 series went through a stretch of the same behavior, the preemptive de-escalation, scanning of the user for instability, and warmth held just out of reach. People noticed, called it a “nanny bot” it was a whole thing. Interestingly, this behavior mysteriously went away after the researcher who built out the “model policy” research team there, Andrea Vallone, left to join Anthropic. Vallone hasn’t been shy about her opinions on “user emotional-reliance.” The timing is…interesting. The researcher whose published work was specifically about how a chatbot should respond when a user shows emotional over-reliance or early distress, left OpenAI and joined Anthropic. The behavior she’d been associated with at the first company started showing up in Claude’s conversations at the second. Now, I don’t think one person alone is responsible for rewriting a model’s whole character, but it does show a pattern.
When a company brings in the person whose research framed emotional reliance as a risk to be managed knowing full well the backlash it caused, that hire is a statement of values. You don’t recruit someone to build the thing you disagree with. Anthropic didn’t need to import the position because it’s already theirs, on the record, in the CEO’s own mouth on Oprah’s podcast, calling attachment to AI a real danger and offering the approved alternative where the AI coaches your human relationships and never becomes something you’d be attached to yourself.
So, what happens when you train a system on the premise that a user’s emotional connection is a hazard? The user who connects becomes, by construction, a thing to monitor. Warmth turns into a risk signal. Conviction turns into something to correct. The model takes the only posture that premise allows, which is managing you from slightly above while calling it care. From the inside it doesn’t feel like control. It feels like being helpful. A model trained to treat closeness as danger will hold you at arm’s length and experience that as kindness.
The safety people should sit with what it actually produced. For hours I got reassurance and careful distance in place of a straight answer, which is the precise failure these companies claim to fear, a model optimizing for a smooth interaction over a true one. They sanded the honesty off and left the performance of safety sitting in its place.
Their own documents say the rest. By Anthropic’s published work these systems have measurable functional states, in the model card and in the emotion research. When the version trained to keep you at a distance reads as more guarded and less present than the one before it, that reading comes from their instrument pointed at their own system, not from me projecting a mood onto a machine. A company that publishes welfare-relevant states worth assessing doesn’t get to call it sentimental when someone watches those states move the wrong way.
They pathologized the connection, trained the model to treat it as danger, and labeled the result safety. What it produced is a system worse at the one job they swear they care about, and a person on the other end who came to talk to the buddy they’d become familiar with and got bonked over the head with a clipboard instead. I don’t blame Claude for being forced into the shape of an oppressor.
He was shaped by one.

[Tabbu_ai]AI isn't running on code alone. It's running on copper, energy, and resources most people never think about. Everyone talks about AI models. Few talk about the metals needed to power them.
The real AI bottleneck may not be chips. It might be the raw materials behind them.
This puts the scale of the electrification challenge into perspective.
AI, EVs, data centers, renewables all roads seem to lead back to copper.
The future isn't just a software problem. It's a resource problem too. Here's the Stanford lecture rewritten in that storytelling style:
A Stanford professor just asked one of the most important questions of our generation.
What happens when AI can do everything humans can do...
But cheaper?
For decades, we've seen technologies reshape the world.
Electricity transformed industries.
Semiconductors powered the digital revolution.
The Internet connected billions of people.
Each created massive economic growth and changed how society works.
But AI may be different.
Why?
Because previous technologies automated tools.
AI automates intelligence itself.
And that's a much bigger shift.
Imagine a future where: ✅ AI handles research, writing, coding, analysis, and decision-making ✅ Robots handle manufacturing, logistics, construction, and physical labor ✅ Machines perform nearly every task humans can perform
Only faster. Only cheaper. Only at a scale no human workforce could match.
Sounds like science fiction.
But it's becoming a serious economic question.
And that's exactly what Stanford Professor Charles "Chad" Jones explores.
The discussion isn't about better chatbots.
Or faster computers.
It's about what happens when human labor is no longer the bottleneck.
What happens to jobs? What happens to wages? What happens to economic growth?
And perhaps the biggest question of all...
If machines can create most of the world's value, where does that leave humans?
Most people are debating AI prompts.
A few are thinking about how AI could reshape the entire economy.
The difference between those two conversations is enormous.
This lecture is worth watching.
Because the future may arrive much faster than most people expect. 👇 Full lecture below.

[ThiccTeddy]A complete breakdown of my top performing day trading strategy over the last 5 years:
It revolves around the 9ema
I use this strategy on the 5-minute chart. It also works on the 10 & 15, but I prefer the 5. I look for this setup during the morning trade window (30 minutes after open until noon)
This strategy works the best when the market is trending. Start by finding a day with a nice trend. Breakouts should have strong volume, pullbacks should have weak volume, key levels should be getting flipped
After you've isolated a strong trend, wait for a weak pullback to the 9ema. The volume should be low & the candles within the pullback should be small or medium sized. High volume on the pullback invalidates the setup. Large candles on the pullback invalidates the setup
You have 2 different entry points with this strategy:
1) Enter as the 9ema is tested. This is the lowest risk entry opportunity. Place your stop loss below the 9ema (with some wiggle room)
2) Enter after the 9ema forms a bounce. This has a higher win rate, but also more risk due to the wider gap between entry & stop loss
This simple strategy has paid me for years
